title: From the Neocognitron to CNNs: comparing deep nets with the ventral stream (Bridge to AI)
text:
CHAPTER 8. VISION
SECTION 8.3. FROM THE NEOCOGNITRON TO CNNs: COMPARING DEEP NETWORKS WITH THE VENTRAL STREAM

A bridge in both directions

This section is a dedicated "Bridge to AI" for the vision chapter. It traces how Hubel and Wiesel's discoveries led, through several steps, to the convolutional neural networks that transformed computer vision, and then how those networks came back to neuroscience as models of the visual brain. It is one of the clearest examples of two-way traffic between the fields.

Fukushima's Neocognitron

The first neural network explicitly built on Hubel and Wiesel's hierarchy was designed by Kunihiko Fukushima, a Japanese engineer working at NHK's broadcasting science research laboratories. In 1975 he described the Cognitron, a self-organizing multilayer network, and in 1980 he published the Neocognitron in the journal Biological Cybernetics, with the subtitle "A self-organizing neural network model for a mechanism of pattern recognition unaffected by shift in position."

The Neocognitron consisted of alternating layers of two types of units, named after Hubel and Wiesel's cells:

- S-cells ("simple"): feature-extracting units. Each S-cell had a local receptive field on the previous layer and responded to a particular pattern within it. S-cells in the same "plane" shared the same input weights, so the same feature was detected at every position. This is weight sharing, or convolution.
- C-cells ("complex"): pooling units. Each C-cell received input from a group of S-cells detecting the same feature at nearby positions and responded if any of them were active. This gave tolerance to small shifts.

Stacking several S-C stages produced units at the top that responded to whole patterns (such as handwritten digits) regardless of their position, and tolerated some distortion. Fukushima trained the S-cells with unsupervised, competitive (winner-take-all, Hebbian-like) learning rather than backpropagation; later versions included some supervised elements. The Neocognitron contained, in 1980, the core architecture of a modern convolutional neural network: local receptive fields, shared weights, feature maps, pooling, and a deep hierarchy. What it lacked was an efficient way to train all layers for a specific task.

LeCun and convolutional networks trained by backpropagation

That step came in the late 1980s. Yann LeCun, working at AT&T Bell Laboratories, combined a convolutional architecture with backpropagation (section 7.3). In 1989, LeCun and colleagues published "Backpropagation applied to handwritten zip code recognition," training a network with shared-weight convolutional layers to recognize handwritten digits from US postal zip codes. A refined architecture, LeNet-5, described in a 1998 paper by LeCun, Leon Bottou, Yoshua Bengio, and Patrick Haffner ("Gradient-based learning applied to document recognition"), was used commercially to read handwritten checks; that paper reported that systems of this kind were reading a significant fraction of checks in the United States. LeCun acknowledged the influence of Fukushima and of Hubel and Wiesel.

The ingredients of a modern CNN, in brief:

- Convolutional layer: applies a set of K learned filters, each of size, say, 3 by 3 by C (where C is the number of input channels), at every position of the input, producing K feature maps. The output at position (i, j) for filter k is sum over (u, v, c) of W_k(u, v, c) * X(i+u, j+v, c) + b_k.
- Nonlinearity: typically ReLU, h = max(0, a), applied element-wise; this is analogous to the threshold of a neuron and to the rectification of ON and OFF channels.
- Pooling: reduces spatial resolution, for example by taking the maximum over 2 by 2 neighborhoods, adding tolerance to position.
- Normalization: various normalization layers, related to gain control in the brain.
- Fully connected layers and a softmax output for classification.

Deep learning's breakthrough: AlexNet

For two decades, CNNs were successful in specialized tasks like digit recognition, but other methods dominated general computer vision. That changed in 2012. Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, and Geoffrey Hinton at the University of Toronto trained a large CNN, now known as AlexNet, on the ImageNet dataset, which contained over a million labeled images in 1,000 categories (the ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge, organized by a team including Fei-Fei Li and Olga Russakovsky). AlexNet had about 60 million parameters, used ReLU activations, dropout, and data augmentation, and was trained on two graphics processing units (GPUs). It won the 2012 competition with a top-5 error rate of roughly 15 to 16 percent, far ahead of the second-best entry, which was around 26 percent. This result is widely seen as the start of the deep learning revolution.

Subsequent networks grew deeper and more accurate: VGG (2014), GoogLeNet/Inception (2014), and ResNet (2015, by Kaiming He and colleagues at Microsoft Research), which introduced residual connections that allowed networks with over a hundred layers to be trained. On the ImageNet benchmark, the best networks were soon reported to match or exceed estimates of human performance on the specific classification task, though such comparisons depend heavily on how human performance is measured.

Later, the transformer architecture, originally developed for language (2017), was adapted to vision. The Vision Transformer (ViT, by Alexey Dosovitskiy and colleagues, 2020) divides an image into patches and processes them with self-attention instead of convolution, with fewer built-in assumptions about locality. With enough data, vision transformers match or exceed CNNs. Interestingly, analyses suggest that vision transformers often learn some local, convolution-like processing in early layers anyway.

Deep networks as models of the ventral stream

As CNNs became powerful, neuroscientists asked: do they process images like the brain? Two influential studies in 2014 suggested that, to a surprising degree, they do.

Daniel Yamins, Ha Hong, Charles Cadieu, Ethan Solomon, Darren Seibert, and James DiCarlo, at MIT, published "Performance-optimized hierarchical models predict neural responses in higher visual cortex" in PNAS in 2014. They recorded from many neurons in macaque V4 and IT while monkeys viewed thousands of images of objects. They then trained CNNs to recognize objects and asked how well the activity of units in the networks could predict the responses of the real neurons, using linear regression from network units to each neuron. Key findings:

- Networks that were better at object recognition were better at predicting IT neural responses. Performance on the task and similarity to the brain were correlated.
- The top layers of the network best predicted IT responses, while intermediate layers best predicted V4 responses. The hierarchy of the network roughly corresponded to the hierarchy of the ventral stream.
- The networks were not trained on neural data at all, only on the object recognition task. The match emerged from optimizing for the task.

In the same year, Seyed-Mahdi Khaligh-Razavi and Nikolaus Kriegeskorte published a study comparing many computational models with human fMRI and monkey IT data using representational similarity analysis (RSA). RSA compares the patterns of dissimilarity between responses to pairs of images in a model and in the brain, without needing a direct mapping of units to neurons. They found that a deep CNN trained on object recognition explained IT representations better than other models, especially when its features were reweighted. Other researchers, including Umut Guclu and Marcel van Gerven (2015), reported similar layer-to-area correspondences with human fMRI.

These results led to a research program sometimes called "goal-driven modeling" or "task-optimized modeling": instead of designing models of neural circuits by hand, train networks to perform the tasks that the brain performs, and then compare their internal representations with the brain. The Brain-Score platform, launched by Martin Schrimpf, DiCarlo, and colleagues around 2018, provides a set of benchmarks comparing models with neural and behavioral data from primate vision, ranking hundreds of models.

Using networks to control neurons

If a network is a good model of a brain area, it should be able to predict what stimuli will drive neurons in that area. In 2019, Pouya Bashivan, Kohitij Kar, and James DiCarlo published a study in Science in which they used a CNN model of monkey V4 to synthesize images designed to drive particular V4 neurons more strongly than any natural image they had tested. When shown to the monkeys, many of these synthetic images did indeed drive the target neurons strongly, often beyond the responses to natural images. Also in 2019, Carlos Ponce, Will Xiao, Margaret Livingstone, Gabriel Kreiman, and colleagues used a generative network guided by the responses of real IT neurons (in a closed loop) to evolve images that strongly activated the neurons, producing strange but sometimes recognizable shapes, including face-like features for face-selective cells. These studies show that deep networks can be used not only to describe but also to probe and control brain activity.

Where the analogy breaks down

The similarities between CNNs and the ventral stream are real, but so are the differences. Several well-documented differences:

1. Adversarial examples. In 2013, Christian Szegedy and colleagues showed that tiny, carefully crafted perturbations to an image, invisible to humans, can make a CNN confidently misclassify it. Human vision is far less susceptible to such perturbations (although some studies have reported that adversarial images designed to fool many models can slightly bias human judgments under brief viewing conditions). This suggests that CNNs rely on features that differ from those humans use.

2. Texture versus shape. Robert Geirhos and colleagues reported in 2019 that ImageNet-trained CNNs tend to classify images based on texture more than on shape: an image of a cat shape filled with elephant skin texture tends to be labeled "elephant" by many CNNs, but "cat" by humans. Training on images with randomized textures increased shape bias and robustness.

3. Out-of-distribution generalization. Humans recognize objects under a wide range of conditions, including line drawings, unusual viewpoints, and heavy noise. CNNs often degrade quickly under distortions they were not trained on, although larger models trained on more diverse data have narrowed this gap considerably.

4. Recurrence and feedback. The ventral stream has abundant recurrent connections within areas and feedback connections from higher to lower areas. Standard CNNs are purely feedforward. Experiments suggest that recurrent processing matters for difficult images. Kohitij Kar, Jonas Kubilius, Kailyn Schmidt, Elias Issa, and James DiCarlo reported in 2019 that images that are hard for feedforward CNNs tend to be those for which monkey IT neurons take longer to develop their object-specific responses, consistent with a role for recurrent computation. Recurrent CNN variants, such as CORnet (Kubilius and colleagues, 2018/2019), improve the match to brain data with fewer layers.

5. Learning. CNNs are trained with millions of labeled images and backpropagation. Infants learn to see without labels, from a continuous stream of experience while moving. Self-supervised learning methods, which learn from unlabeled images by predicting parts of an image or by making representations of different views of the same image similar, have produced networks whose representations match ventral stream data about as well as supervised networks. Chengxu Zhuang, Daniel Yamins, and colleagues reported in 2021 that unsupervised (self-supervised) networks could predict ventral stream responses comparably to supervised ones, which supports the idea that the brain could learn its visual representations largely without labels.

6. Biological details. Real neurons spike, have dendrites, and come in many types, with excitatory and inhibitory populations. Retinal input is foveated, and the eyes move several times per second (saccades). CNNs process uniform-resolution images in one glance. Some work has explored adding foveation, eye movements, and biologically inspired front ends to CNNs. For example, Joel Dapello, Tiago Marques, Martin Schrimpf, and colleagues reported in 2020 that adding a fixed front end modeled on V1 (with Gabor filters and noise) to CNNs increased their robustness to adversarial perturbations.

7. Topography. The brain has maps (retinotopic maps, face patches, category-selective regions). CNNs have no spatial layout of units within a layer beyond the feature map grid. Recent work, as mentioned in section 3.3, has shown that adding spatial wiring constraints to networks can produce brain-like topographic organization.

What have we learned?

The CNN story teaches several lessons about the relationship between neuroscience and AI.

First, neuroscience inspired a key architecture. The ideas of local receptive fields, shared weights, and hierarchical pooling came from Hubel and Wiesel through Fukushima. Without this inspiration, CNNs might have been invented anyway (they are also natural from a signal processing perspective), but the historical influence is clear.

Second, engineering made the inspiration work. Large datasets, backpropagation, GPUs, ReLU, and many training techniques were needed. Most of these did not come from neuroscience.

Third, the resulting systems became useful models for neuroscience, though imperfect ones. The fact that task-optimized networks predict neural responses suggests that the brain's visual system can be understood, at least partly, as a solution to the problem of object recognition under constraints. The differences point to what is missing: recurrence, robustness, unsupervised learning, and biological constraints.

Fourth, the comparison is a two-way benchmark. Neuroscience data can be used to evaluate AI models (Brain-Score), and AI models can be used to generate hypotheses and stimuli for neuroscience experiments.

A note on interpretability

Researchers have used methods inspired by neurophysiology to understand what units in CNNs respond to. Matthew Zeiler and Rob Fergus (2014) visualized the patterns that activate units at different layers, finding edge detectors in early layers, textures and patterns in middle layers, and object parts and objects in higher layers, a hierarchy reminiscent of the ventral stream. Work by Chris Olah and colleagues on "feature visualization" and "circuits" analyzed individual neurons and connections in vision networks, finding curve detectors, high-low frequency detectors, and other features, and tracing how they are built from earlier features. This is, in effect, doing Hubel and Wiesel's experiments on an artificial network: presenting stimuli and recording from units. The advantage over neuroscience is that every weight and every unit can be measured exactly, which has made artificial networks a testing ground for methods that neuroscientists might use on the brain.

Summary

- Fukushima's Neocognitron (1980) implemented Hubel and Wiesel's simple-complex hierarchy with shared-weight S-cells and pooling C-cells.
- LeCun's convolutional networks (1989, LeNet-5 in 1998) combined this architecture with backpropagation and were used to read checks.
- AlexNet (2012) won ImageNet by a large margin with a deep CNN trained on GPUs, launching the deep learning era; ResNets and vision transformers followed.
- Task-optimized CNNs predict neural responses in V4 and IT, with layer-to-area correspondence (Yamins et al. 2014; Khaligh-Razavi and Kriegeskorte 2014); Brain-Score benchmarks such models.
- CNN models can synthesize images that drive specific neurons.
- Differences include adversarial vulnerability, texture bias, weaker out-of-distribution generalization, lack of recurrence, supervised training, and missing biological details.
- Interpretability research applies neurophysiology-like methods to artificial networks.
